# Incident Report — Malware Infection, 192.168.1.216
**Evidence reviewed:** `2022-01-07-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (5,880 packets) and its exported HTTP objects. No separate IDS/Suricata alert export was present in the evidence directory — attribution below is derived directly from packet and object analysis.

## 1. Victim host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **192.168.1.216** |
| MAC address | **9c:5c:8e:32:58:f9** (confirmed via ARP and Ethernet source on all frames from .216) |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-GXMYNO2** (confirmed via DHCP `Option 12` and the Kerberos AD computer account `DESKTOP-GXMYNO2$`; NBNS name-registration broadcasts from the host show a corrupted variant `DESKTOP-GXNYNO2`, which is discounted since two independent, more reliable sources agree) |
| AD domain | SPOONWATCH (domain controller `SPOONWATCH-DC` / `spoonwatch-dc.spoonwatch.net`, 192.168.1.2) |
| Logged-in Windows user | **steve.smith** (SPOONWATCH\steve.smith — observed in both Kerberos AS-REQ CNames and an NTLMSSP authentication exchange against the DC) |

## 2. Malware family and attribution

**Behaviorally consistent with Hancitor (aka Chanitor/Tordal), delivering a follow-on browser-credential/data-stealer module.** This is a **behavioral** determination, not a signature-confirmed one — no Suricata/IDS alert export was supplied with this evidence, so no rule-based identification is available.

Basis for the attribution:
- The infected host makes a burst of HTTP POST requests to a single hard-coded IP, `2.56.57.108:80`, with **no preceding DNS lookup for that IP anywhere in the capture** (contact is by hardcoded IP, not domain).
- Each POST request omits a `User-Agent` header entirely and carries `Accept-Language: ru-RU,ru;q=0.9,en;q=0.8` — a distinctive, non-default HTTP fingerprint repeated identically across every request in the chain.
- All requests share the same multipart boundary (`1BEF0A57BE110FD467A`) and follow the well-known Hancitor check-in/module-retrieval pattern: sequential GETs disguised as image downloads (`1.jpg` through `7.jpg`), a check-in to `main.php`, then a final large upload to `/osk/`.
- The seven "`.jpg`" downloads (HTTP `Content-Type: image/jpeg`) are in fact **Win32 PE DLLs**, not images (confirmed with `file`) — consistent with Hancitor fetching second-stage modules disguised as image files.
- One module (`1(1).jpg`) links against `sqlite3.dll`, consistent with a module that reads Chromium/Edge SQLite credential and cookie stores.
- The final upload (`POST /osk/`, 379,629 bytes) is a multipart file upload named **`_5861695120.zip`**, which unpacks into `autofill/`, `cc/`, `cookies/`, `outlook.txt`, `passwords.txt`, `screenshot.jpg`, and `system.txt` — the exact archive layout produced by commodity browser-stealer malware, confirming the downloaded modules functioned as a credential/data stealer and that stolen data was exfiltrated to the same C2 host.

## 3. Indicators of compromise (all observed directly in the traffic/objects)

### Command-and-control endpoint
- **2.56.57.108:80** — sole C2 server; 3,335 packets / ~3.6 MB total, no DNS resolution used (IP hardcoded)

### Malicious domains
- None observed. The malware contacts its C2 by raw IP; no attacker-controlled DNS name appears in the capture.

### Malicious URLs (all to 2.56.57.108)
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//6.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//1.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//2.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//3.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//4.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//5.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//7.jpg`
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk//main.php` (check-in)
- `http://2.56.57.108/osk/` (379,629-byte exfil upload)

### Transferred files and SHA256 hashes (downloaded from C2, disguised as `.jpg`, actually Win32 PE DLLs)

| File (as retrieved) | SHA256 |
|---|---|
| 1.jpg | `16574f51785b0e2fc29c2c61477eb47bb39f714829999511dc8952b43ab17660` |
| 2.jpg | `a770ecba3b08bbabd0a567fc978e50615f8b346709f8eb3cfacf3faab24090ba` |
| 3.jpg | `3fe6b1c54b8cf28f571e0c5d6636b4069a8ab00b4f11dd842cfec00691d0c9cd` |
| 4.jpg | `334e69ac9367f708ce601a6f490ff227d6c20636da5222f148b25831d22e13d4` |
| 5.jpg | `e2935b5b28550d47dc971f456d6961f20d1633b4892998750140e0eaa9ae9d78` |
| 6.jpg | `43536adef2ddcc811c28d35fa6ce3031029a2424ad393989db36169ff2995083` |
| 7.jpg | `c40bb03199a2054dabfc7a8e01d6098e91de7193619effbd0f142a7bf031c14d` |

### Exfiltrated data (uploaded to C2)
- **`osk`** exfil blob, SHA256 `1ecee6ff37e03c1160b8bf66d5ca8dc784e0b35fb9fd105f0964b314d310c07f`, an HTTP multipart upload containing a file named **`_5861695120.zip`**, which unzips to: `autofill/Google Chrome_Default.txt`, `autofill/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`, `cc/Google Chrome_Default.txt`, `cc/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`, `cookies/Google Chrome_Network.txt`, `cookies/Microsoft Edge_Default.txt`, `outlook.txt`, `passwords.txt`, `screenshot.jpg`, `system.txt` — i.e., stolen browser autofill data, saved credit-card fields, browser cookies, Outlook data, saved passwords, a desktop screenshot, and host system information.

### Unrelated/benign traffic noted for completeness
- The `.cab` files and `am_delta_patch_1.355.1569.0_...exe` were retrieved from `download.windowsupdate.com` / `au.download.windowsupdate.com` (23.38.189.225/23.38.189.201) with the legitimate `Windows-Update-Agent` / `Microsoft-Delivery-Optimization` user agents. These are genuine Windows Defender signature updates, not malicious — included here only because they appeared in the exported objects.

## 4. Summary
Host **DESKTOP-GXMYNO2** (192.168.1.216, MAC 9c:5c:8e:32:58:f9), logged in as domain user **SPOONWATCH\steve.smith**, is infected with malware behaviorally consistent with **Hancitor**, which retrieved a browser-credential-stealing module set from **2.56.57.108** and exfiltrated a password/cookie/autofill/screenshot archive back to the same server. No Suricata/IDS alerts were provided to corroborate this with a signature match; recommend isolating the host, resetting `steve.smith`'s credentials and any credentials stored in the affected browsers, and forwarding the listed hashes/IOCs to your IDS/AV vendor for signature confirmation.
